FD-TD directly solves Maxwell's curl equations using second-order central differences in space and time.
Typical FD-TD spatial discretization uses 10 to 20 cells per wavelength for accuracy.
Time step size is chosen to satisfy a stability condition related to the maximum wave velocity.
Number of sinusoidal cycles needed to reach steady state depends on target electrical size and Q factor.
For a target spanning 10 wavelengths, about 40 cycles (800 time steps at 10 cells/wavelength) are needed for steady state.
FD-TD uses a total-field/scattered-field lattice division to efficiently simulate incident and scattered waves.
Stepped-edge approximation is used for curved surfaces by assigning material parameters component-wise to lattice cells.
Radiation boundary conditions at lattice truncation planes minimize nonphysical reflections of outgoing waves.
FD-TD modeling of a square metal cylinder (k0s=2) showed surface current magnitude agreement within ±1% and phase within ±3° compared to MOM solutions.
A muscle-fat-layered cylinder model at 100 MHz with cell size 1.5 cm showed excellent agreement with analytical solutions despite stepped-edge approximations.
FD-TD can model anisotropic materials by specifying permittivity, permeability, and conductivity independently for each field component.
Computational storage and runtime scale linearly with the number of unknown field components in the modeled volume.
Near-field to far-field transformations are performed using tangential scattered fields on a fixed rectangular observation surface in the scattered-field region.
FD-TD has been validated on canonical 2D and 3D targets including metal cubes, plates, and T-shaped conductors.
The method is robust for modeling multiple scattering, penetration through apertures, and cavity excitations.
FD-TD avoids subtraction noise in low-field regions, enabling near-field computational dynamic ranges exceeding 60 dB.
Advances in FD-TD theory and supercomputer technology are expected to enhance modeling of electrically large and complex targets.

FD-TD time stepping is explicit, requiring no solution of simultaneous linear equations.
The method naturally satisfies tangential field continuity at media interfaces without special matching.
